Lense.ai

Thematic and human factors analysis of incident and investigation reports. For any set of reports, Lense.ai identifies the themes and contributory factors that recur across them, and extracts the key facts from each report — every finding traceable to its source sentences.

How it works

Developed at Loughborough University by a research group specialising in AI and the analysis of incident reports.

About the archive supplied with the tool. Prevention of Future Deaths reports are written by coroners and published by the Judiciary, which remains the authoritative source. Lense.ai does not alter them.

Capabilities

What the tool does

Every capability applies at any scale: the whole archive of more than 6,300 reports, a search within the archive, or a project built from selected reports.

Maintained automatically

Every published report and its responses, collected from the judiciary website each night.

Full-text and semantic search

Full-text search of every report, including scanned reports, and search by meaning.

Filtering

Category, healthcare speciality, NHS region, coroner and date, applied in any combination.

Dashboards and trends

Charts of any project, search or the whole archive, with factors and themes tracked across years.

Projects

Shared working sets of reports, able to hold an organisation’s own reports on request.

Contributory factors

The Matters of Concern annotated against the 19 Yorkshire framework factors, open to review.

Thematic analysis

Themes generated from the text of the reports, specific to each project.

Structured extraction

More than 20 fields from each report — demographics and Equality Act characteristics, dates, coroner and NHS region, cause of death, conditions and drugs, hospitals and recipients — each value linked to its evidence.

How it works

From access to analysis

1

Individual access

Access is by individual account with a personal password. Each account belongs to one person, so every project and every review decision traces to a named person.

2

The archive is supplied and current

The full archive is available from the first login — every report, searchable in full text or by meaning, and filterable by category, healthcare speciality, NHS region, coroner, and date of report or of death. Opening a report shows its key facts, the evidence behind each fact, and the original documents. Each report’s published responses are attached to it, and the source is checked nightly, so the archive stays current.

home birth
9 reports found
Reports containing the exact words “home birth”.
Found 146 relevant reports+46 reports containing the exact search but seemingly unrelated
Searched the following expanded topic — Home birth: a death primarily concerning home birth, planned home delivery, domiciliary childbirth, intrapartum complications during home birth, failure to recognise obstetric emergencies at home, or delayed transfer from home to hospital.
Every result carries a relevance badge: Keyword contains the exact words; Semantic is about the topic but worded differently.
3

Gather reports into a project

Search or filter for the reports relevant to a question, a service, a population or a coroner area, and place them in a named project. The project is private to its owner, who can share it with any other account holder.

4

Factor annotation: the analysis is already in place

The Matters of Concern in every report are annotated automatically against the Yorkshire Contributory Factors on the night the report is collected, and every factor is linked to its supporting sentences. Within a project, a reviewer can view the factors and add supporting sentences to them from any part of the report.

The reviewer holds the decision. Every factor carries Accept, Reject and Relabel controls, and the archive and the analytics use the reviewer’s decision.

5

Factor analysis: the contributory factors in charts

The contributory factors are aggregated across the reports in a project: which factors occur most, how each has moved over time, and how they distribute across the report categories and coroner areas.

6

Theme annotation: agreeing the themes in each report

The tool reads the reports in the project and groups the concerns they raise into themes. The reviewer accepts or rejects each theme for the project.

7

Theme analysis: the themes across the project

The accepted themes are charted across the project: which themes occur most, how each trends over time, and how they distribute across the report categories. A co-occurrence matrix counts the reports that carry any two themes together.

8

Key facts extracted from each report

Demographics, cause of death and mentions of the Equality Act 2010 characteristics are extracted from each report, every value carrying the sentence it came from and open to correction by a reviewer.

9

Visualisation and export

The dashboard charts whatever is currently selected: the whole archive, a search, or a chosen project — select a project and every chart re-draws for its reports. Reports over time can be viewed by day, week or month, by date of report or date of death, and themes can be tracked across years or cross-tabulated against categories. Every chart's data downloads as CSV, and each project's extracted data downloads as one Excel workbook: a Dataset sheet with more than 60 columns per report, plus an evidence tab for every field, each value linked to its evidence.

10

Project activity and tracking

A project flags new reports collected overnight that match its latest search, and shows each member’s review progress. The activity log keeps a dated record of every change, and any past search can be re-opened and run again.

The archive

The Prevention of Future Deaths archive, and who it concerns

Every report in the archive follows an inquest into a person's death. This shapes how the tool is built: the report is never altered, every finding carries the wording it came from, and a human reviewer decides whether it stands.

A coroner addresses the report to the organisations with the power to prevent a similar death: councils, police forces, prisons, government departments, schools, transport operators, manufacturers and regulators, as well as NHS trusts.

Accuracy

Measured against human experts on 130 coroners' reports

The annotation was compared, factor by factor, against 130 reports annotated by a senior human factors expert with long experience of this framework, and by a researcher he trained for more than a year. Every disagreement was checked against the report text.

88%Agreementtool and human expert reached the same conclusion
0.68Cohen's kappaagreement corrected for chance; a substantial level
81%Recallof the factors the experts recorded were also identified by the tool
70%Precisionof the factors the tool identified were confirmed correct

The tool also identified further relevant factors that were confirmed on review, which is the purpose of combining automated annotation with human oversight.

When the tool and the experts disagreed, the definitions were sharpened where the framework's categories overlapped. Expert judgement shaped the tool, and the tool does not replace that judgement.

Developed on expert annotation

The AI was developed and refined using coroners' reports annotated by human factors experts. Their annotations set the definitions, supplied the worked examples and remain the standard against which the tool is measured.

Human review continues in use: any factor can be accepted, rejected or relabelled, and reviewed decisions take precedence.

Meet the team

Meet the team

Analysing incident reports takes two things: the AI that reads them at scale, and the human factors expertise that decides what a contributory factor is and whether it has been found. The tool was built by a team of researchers in both fields.

Computer scientists

Professor Georgina Cosma

Project lead · Computer Science/AI

Georgina Cosma is Professor of AI and Data Science at Loughborough University, where she leads the Neural Information Processing, Retrieval and Modelling research group. She holds a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Warwick. Her research spans natural language processing and large language models, neural and cross-modal information retrieval, and their application to healthcare, developed throughout on responsible AI principles. She leads the research and design of Lense.ai.

Dr Mikel Williams Lekuona

AI Software Engineer

Dr Mikel Williams Lekuona is an AI Engineer at Loughborough University, where he leads the software development of the project. He holds a PhD in multimodal AI, having authored peer-reviewed research on image-text retrieval. His work spans the full stack of applied AI systems: production LLM integration, hybrid semantic search, and evaluation methods that keep machine outputs grounded and auditable. He specialises in turning research prototypes into deployed, production-grade platforms, translating technically complex systems into tools that research and healthcare teams can use.

Krina Vara

AI Software Engineer · Human-factors trained

Krina Vara is a researcher and AI software developer at Loughborough University, where she co-developed the tool and led its evaluation. She holds a first-class MSci in Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence and was trained in human factors by Professor Waterson. Her work spans annotation pipelines for incident reports, their preparation at scale, and the evaluation of language models against expert human annotation. She specialises in search and data visualisation, turning the analysis of thousands of reports into a form in which patterns can be seen.

Human factors specialists

Professor Patrick Waterson

Human factors lead

Patrick Waterson is Professor of Human Factors and Complex Systems at Loughborough University, a Chartered Psychologist and Fellow of the Chartered Institute of Ergonomics and Human Factors, and Editor-in-Chief of Ergonomics. His research applies human factors and systems thinking to safety in healthcare and other complex domains. He has annotated several hundred coroners’ reports against the Yorkshire Contributory Factors, providing the expert annotation on which the tool was developed and evaluated.

Professor Gyuchan Thomas Jun

Human factors

Gyuchan Thomas Jun is Professor of Sociotechnical System Design at Loughborough University and a Chartered Ergonomist and Human Factors Specialist. His research applies systems thinking to the design of complex healthcare systems and the integration of new technologies — digital health, machine learning and wearables — into them. He co-founded the University’s Human Factors and Complex Systems research group and leads its Systems Thinking Lab.

Social good

Developed for social good — and open to partners

Lense.ai is developed and operated for social good by a research group at Loughborough University, supported by a Loughborough University Impact Accelerator Award. It is free to use.

Who we would like to work with

Prevention of Future Deaths reports reach every part of public life, and partnership is open to every sector: the public sector, industry, the third sector, and academia.

A partnership can start small — a shared project on the reports in your remit, or an analysis run together — and grow into co-designed features and joint studies.

Partner with us

If your organisation works with these reports, or with incident reports of its own, we would like to hear what you need from them — and to show you what the tool can already do.

Discuss a partnership

Acknowledging the tool

If Lense.ai contributes to your work, two things help us in return

What keeps Lense.ai maintained is evidence that it is used — so we ask for a brief mention in the work it supports, and a short note telling us what you used it for.

In a report or a presentation

The analysis was carried out using Lense.ai, developed at Loughborough University by Georgina Cosma, Patrick Waterson, Mikel Williams Lekuona and Krina Vara (doi:10.17028/rd.lboro.33011351).

In a publication

Cosma G, Waterson P, Williams Lekuona M, Vara K. Lense.ai: thematic and human factors analysis of incident and investigation reports [Software]. Loughborough University; 2026. doi:10.17028/rd.lboro.33011351

Tell us what you used it for

Tell us what you were trying to find out, and whether the tool helped. If the tool did not do what you needed, that is the most useful message we get — it is how the tool improves.

There is a feedback form in the tool, or you can email Professor Georgina Cosma directly — including if you’d like to learn more. We never name a user or an organisation without asking first.
